title: Jaidev, the old poet
hookLine: the poet of the Gita Govinda has two hymns in the Granth (Gujri, Jaidev, ang 526)

lines: A LOVE POEM: KRISHNA AND RADHA.
THE SAME NAME IN RAAG GUJRI.
cards: The Gita Govinda is a love poem in Sanskrit about Krishna and Radha: longing, quarrels, reunion in the forest by the river. Its poet is Jaidev.
Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to Raag Gujri, Ang 526, and there's that same name at the head of a hymn. It isn't the only one: Jaidev has two hymns in the Granth.
The singer of the forest romance, on the same pages as the Gurus.

teach.h: AN OLDER ACCENT: SANSKRIT IN THE SOUND.
teach.b: Start with how the Gujri hymn sounds. Its language leans hard on Sanskrit, the old learned tongue, so when it's sung it has a different ring from the Punjabi and Hindi around it. Same book, older accent.

In paraphrase: the Lord was there before everything, beyond compare, true, lovely beyond telling, beyond nature itself. Then the turn: chant only the Name of the Lord, sweet, the very essence of nectar.

teach.h: THE NAME, AND NO FEAR OF DEATH.
teach.b: Remember Him, and the fear of birth, old age and death no longer has a hold. Then he gets practical. He asks for purity in three places at once: in what you do, what you say, and what you think.

teach.h: PURE IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT.
teach.b: All of them, lined up. Set that beside his fame.
The poet of a lush romance of gods in a forest is kept in the Granth for something spare: one Lord, beyond compare, and the Name.

The hymn even asks, in paraphrase, what yoga, sacrifice, charity or austerity are worth beside that devotion. Some readers hear the Gurus keeping the part of an old poet's voice that rings with their own.
Others say simply that the Granth honors devotion wherever it was sung. Either way, an old name sits on the page, sung in the same kirtan as everything else, asking for one life lined up three ways.

how: Jaidev's hymns are sung in kirtan in Raag Gujri and Raag Maru like other Gurbani, and Sikh readers hear in them the remembrance of the one Lord and the Name.

o: the hero of a love story about Krishna
the Gita Govinda poet, with hymns in the Granth
a Sikh Guru who wrote in old Sanskrit

games.q: inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: Jaidev's love poem of Krishna and Radha
the three places to be pure

s: Jaidev's hymn in the Granth retells Krishna and Radha
it praises the one Lord beyond compare and the sweet Name.
the Gujri hymn sounds close to Sanskrit
its language leans on Sanskrit, so it rings differently from the Punjabi around it.
the hymn asks for purity only in thought
it asks for purity in deed, word and thought together.

games.q: you're compiling a holy book and come across a well-known poet of a forest romance of the gods. what do you keep?
o: his hymns of the one Lord and the Name.
games.why: the Granth keeps Jaidev's hymns of the Lord beyond compare and the Name, sung in kirtan like the rest.

practice: Take Jaidev's three places, one per breath. On the first, look at something you did today; on the next, something you said; on the next, something you thought, gently, and keep the cycle going.
If you pray, let Waheguru close each round.
